Warning! The following contains spoilers for the The Circle series premiere on Hulu "Welcome To The Circle." Stream it with a Hulu subscription, or read at your own risk!

The Circle's Hulu premiere dropped this past Tuesday, and it was mostly what I hoped it would be. For starters, I was right that adding celebrities to the mix made the start of the season even better to watch. That said, there is one thing I really miss in comparison to the long-running version I enjoyed with my Netflix subscription, but I'm willing to continue watching despite that.

Michelle Buteau served as The Circle's host for all of its original run on Netflix, but as we knew ahead of its premiere on the 2026 TV schedule, she wasn't invited for this new installment. I didn't think it would be a big deal before watching the premiere, but I have to admit, I really miss her.

Buteau, who readers may know from her Netflix series Survival of the Thickest, was more than just a narrator for The Circle. She brought a lot of comedy to the game, which I felt was a little lacking in Hulu's premiere. Buteau's personality helped shape the tone of the show, which helped make it one of the best reality series.

During the premiere, I couldn't help but feel like I was watching American Idol without Ryan Seacrest. That feels like a problem, because while Hulu clearly felt The Circle needed retooling for its new era, the show lasted seven seasons for a reason. Again, I still enjoyed the episode, but there was no denying that there was a definite shift in tone due to the comic's absence.

It may just take time for me to get used to Tinx (Christina Najjar), who comes into The Circle with plenty of experience elsewhere. Before she was hosting the Hulu series, the influencer rose to fame through her no-nonsense advice. This evolved into a podcast, a New York Times best-selling book and a deal with SiriusXM.

I Can't Stop Thinking About The Circle's AI Twist And I Have So Many Feelings

Tinx has the resume for the role, but one episode in, I don't really see the same personality in her that I saw in Michelle Buteau. Granted, it's been one episode, and if we were all judged by our first day on the job, many of us would probably in trouble.

Nevertheless, the role of host on The Circle is very critical, so I hope I get used to it sooner rather than later. There's already so much happening after the first episode, and we need someone who can navigate all the craziness that will unfold over these next few weeks before the $100,000 winner is crowned.

Catch new episodes of The Circle on Hulu on Tuesdays, Wednesdays, and Thursdays at 9:00 p.m. ET. I'm eager to see this new format in action, and I'm ready for an audience vote to really shake things up as we get underway!

He graduated from the University of Southern Indiana with a degree in Journalism and a minor in Radio and Television. He's great at hosting panels and appearing on podcasts if given the chance as well.

#3789. The Game Awards just confirmed who plays GTA 6's Lucia

Manni L. Perez has been confirmed as the actress behind Grand Theft Auto 6's Lucia Caminos, just days before the game launches.

As spotted by IGN, the confirmation came during The Game Awards' nominations livestream today, where Perez was nominated for Best Performance for her role as co-lead Lucia.

Perez had been widely rumoured to play Lucia for months, and fans have regularly filled her social media livestreams with questions about GTA 6, which she has been oh-so-carefully sidestepping.

Lucia is one half of GTA 6's lead pair alongside Jason Duval, making it the first Grand Theft Auto game with a playable couple.

Jason's actor wasn't among the nominees, so who plays him is still a mystery.

Perez has previously had guest roles in a string of US TV dramas, including Law & Order: Special Victims Unit, Chicago P.D., The Blacklist, and Blindspot, and has also done voice work for GTA Online.

Funnily enough, Lucia isn't her first Lucia - she also played Lucia Santiago in a 2023 episode of CBS's East New York.

GTA 6 arrives 19th November on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. It is now available to pre-load for anyone who pre-ordered the digital version, and those with the code-in-box physical version.

It's long been revealed that GTA 6 will have a regional release, meaning that some lucky, soon-to-be players will be able to access the game much earlier than others. Rockstar's regional release schedule sees the game launching at midnight on 19th November regardless of what region you're in, and if you wish to join those playing almost a day early, there's the good ol' Xbox New Zealand trick for eager players to try.

#3788. PC remains GTA 6's last hope for 60fps smoothness as Rockstar confirm such an option isn't coming to even the swankiest consoles

Poor little game boxes just can't handle it

As you've probably heard, GTA 6 is out on consoles this week and targeting 30 FPS on that hardware. Despite reports claiming one may not be far away, there's still no official word on a PC port, hence why we've not got a review that delves deep into analysis of just how central to the experience the smell reaction system is.

The wait for confirmation of a PC version continues, then, and it looks like that might well be the only chance people get to play the crime sandbox at 60fps, with Rockstar having confirmed that higher frame rate modes aren't en-route to even the most beefy of consoles.

Speaking to Kotaku, GTA 6's devs made clear optional 60 or 40fps performance modes aren't on the way, even for the more powerful Pro variant of the PS5.

"Our base presentation makes use of ray-traced reflections and global illumination. On the PS5 Pro, this is enhanced with the addition of ray-traced shadows, as well as overall added clarity through the use of PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR)," Rockstar technology production director Marc Chambers put it. "The PS5 Pro features an upgraded graphics processor and upscaling technology that we leverage to increase the game’s visual fidelity. While the PS5 Pro’s central processor is slightly better than the PS5 base console, it is not powerful enough to run the game’s complex simulation at higher frame rates."

So, there you go. The consoles just ain't got that dog in 'em. One would think, then, that being able to run GTA 6 in all its glory at higher frame rates will likely be a selling point for that PC port that's assumed to be on the way. Whether the average PC owner's graphics card and other bits will have the horses to deliver a smooth 60 is another question, and an especially pertinent one given the ongoing RAM crisis has made upgrading certain aspects of your setup ludicrously expensive.

If it requires a 5090 at a minimum, I guess those of us with less than absolute cutting edge cards will just have to keep playing Sleeping Dogs until the AI bubble bursts.

Much like its predecessors, GTA 6 plays home to countless Easter eggs – many of which I'm certain fans will uncover in the coming days – including a potential little nod to Rockstar co-founder Sam Houser himself.

Warning – this article contains spoilers for the third chapter of Grand Theft Auto 6.

In case you've not seen it yet (and, just as a precautionary warning, this is a bit of a spoiler if you haven't completed the accompanying mission "Boobie Time" in Chapter 3), it's nothing major, really – but it's a nice Easter egg that comes up sort of unexpectedly. You can see it play out over on YouTube, when Jason connects with Boobie Ike and we see… well, Sam Houser. Or, as he's dubbed in-game, "Little Sam."

I won't say much more about the mission in its entirety myself, but some folks have caught wind of the reference to the Rockstar lead already, taking to forums like Reddit to point out his presence in the new GTA. One person points out how "they even call him Little Sam and say he doesn't talk much," while another posts a screenshot from Grand Theft Auto 3 – one that depicts minor character "Sam," long-rumored to be Sam Houser.

I'm excited to see what other Easter eggs pop up as more players explore the depths of Vice City in GTA 6, honestly. We're sure to see some throwbacks, references to other big games (perhaps some Red Dead Redemption 2 nods as well), and more, knowing Rockstar. The game has only just landed in players' hands, though – but something tells me it won't be too long before we see Easter egg roundups surface online.

I'm personally keeping my own fingers crossed for some more niche indie tidbits here and there, just for fun – and humor, of course, but I think Rockstar nails that outside of its Easter eggs well enough already.

The aim-assisting PureVector technology in this mouse promises a lot, but in my case it fails to deliver, as my aim doesn't improve from turning it on. It's a solid, lightweight, competitive mouse regardless, but it's too expensive for what it is without delivering the PureVector promise.

PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware.

Corsair is continuing the 2026 trend of brands pushing out new and innovative mouse technologies. In this case, it's all in the 'PureVector' part of the name. In partnership with AimLabs, Corsair has made a mouse that can adjust sensitivity in different directions to tailor it to your movements and help you aim better.

That's the claim, anyway. In practice, I've found that PureVector hasn't improved my aim, both subjectively while gaming and objectively based on multiple AimLabs tests. Some pro players that Corsair highlights claim it's helped them, so your mileage may vary.

Apart from PureVector, though, the mouse itself deserves some attention, as it's still a very performant, lightweight mouse for competitive gaming. It has some upgrades compared to its predecessor, the Sabre V2 Pro, too.

✅ You want to try the latest tech: You might get better results than I did with PureVector. It tailors sensor sensitivity in different directions based on how you aim.

❌ You want good value for the basics: If you just want a comfy mouse with solid build quality that performs well, you can find something of better value elsewhere.

The aim-assisting PureVector technology in this mouse promises a lot, but in my case it fails to deliver, as my aim doesn't improve from turning it on. It's a solid, lightweight, competitive mouse regardless, but it's too expensive for what it is without delivering on the PureVector promise.

Replacement skates, USB-A to USB-C cable, wireless dongle, AimLabs PureVector software integration

In most ways, the Sabre V3 Pro PureVector Ergo is your standard competitive gaming mouse: lightweight, few frills, simple design, good sensor. It is lighter than most competitive mice with a solid shell, though a little heavier than its predecessor, the Sabre V2 Pro.

Setting aside the PureVector aiming shenanigans for a moment, probably the biggest improvement compared to the Sabre V2 Pro is its battery life, which has been doubled. Apart from that, you're getting a 42,000 DPI sensor, optical clicks, and some bigger replacement skates included in the box.

Now we come to the main attraction: PureVector. Corsair has designed the mouse's internals and firmware to permit different sensitivities in different directions. So, for instance, it can move slightly slower horizontally than vertically.

Corsair has worked with AimLabs to let you test your aiming in the latter software and then have the mouse adjust your directional sensitivity for you. The PureVector software within AimLabs has been made with the help of a bunch of aiming data (over 4 billion data points, apparently) and machine learning. The end result is, in theory, a mouse that can tailor its sensitivity in different directions to stop you over-shooting or under-shooting your target.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

Again, in theory, this should also save you time when you aim, and Corsair claims it can save more time than reducing the latency of clicks—the latter is, for example, what we see the Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike and X3 Superstrike focusing on.

It's worth noting that Corsair highlights a number of pro players who say they've benefitted from this new tech. However, for my part, I haven't noticed a difference.

For reference, I play Counter-Strike 2 at about FaceIt Level 7 or Premier 18–20,000 rating (approx. top 25%). I'm far from a pro, but I'm far from the worst. In-game, I didn't notice any difference between my aim with PureVector set up and with it disabled.

I also repeatedly tested my aim in the AimLabs SpiderShot Precision test, and I actually had slightly better results using another mouse without PureVector (the SteelSeries Sensei Pro), and the latter mouse my hand was less familiar with.

More than this, though, I can't help but feel that it's a bit of a band-aid solution to poor aim. If you're overshooting your shots when you aim left, for instance, you could get PureVector to lower your sensitivity in that direction. But why not instead work on training your hand not to overshoot? That way, having good aim won't be dependent on using this one mouse, and you can get used to aiming consistently in different directions.

PureVector aside, the Sabre V3 Pro performs well. The sensor is great and feels very responsive. Ditto the new optical mouse clicks. I have no complaints about its performance as a general mouse, I just don't see the use in PureVector myself. Of course, your mileage may vary, as it seems to have for some pro players.

One area where the Sabre V3 Pro does particularly shine, just like the Sabre V2 Pro, is in its light weight. This latest iteration feels even sturdier than the previous one and still manages to be lighter than most competitive gaming mice.

Battery life is a definite selling point of the Sabre V3 Pro PureVector. It's a lot better than I was expecting. The Sabre V2 Pro can only manage about 70 hours at 1 kHz, and this new one doubles that to 140 hours.

I think Corsair has struck a great balance here, because it's not as light as the V2—which was 36 g—but 41 g is still incredibly light, and I'd much rather have the bigger battery than shave off those few extra grams. You're not getting any fancy wireless charging or hot-swappable batteries here, but 140 hours of battery life is great.

The Corsair Sabre V3 Pro PureVector Ergo is, as its excruciatingly long name suggests, pretty ergonomic. It's not the biggest ergo mouse I've used—the Zowie EC2-DW and SteelSeries Rival Pro both feel a bit bigger in-hand—but it still feels comfy under my medium-sized palm.

There's also a non-ergo, symmetrical version for the same price, and you can get carbon fiber or magnesium versions for each, if you're willing to spend even more ($200 and $230, respectively).

I like the lightweight ergonomic version, though. Its slightly smaller size, combined with its light weight, also means holding it in a fingertip or claw grip doesn't feel too bad, which isn't something you can say about many ergonomic mice. Palm grip is still the main intention here, though. Playing Counter-Strike on low sensitivity feels great.

Build quality is decent, too, which is a bit of a relief because the previous version, the Sabre V2 Pro, sacrificed some on this front to achieve its 'ultralight' status. There's no creak or flex along the sides, and only a slight bit of flex on the underside. The side buttons feel great, with no pre-travel, and the scroll wheel has well-defined steps.

There is some pre-travel to the left- and right-mouse buttons, however, and they don't feel as satisfying to press as some other mice like the Razer Viper V4 Pro or SteelSeries Rival Pro. They're far from bad, just not quite up to the standard of some other expensive gaming mice I've tried.

The version I've got here, the 'Ergo' one, is pretty plain and looks quite similar to its predecessor, the Sabre V2 Pro. It's plain white, with only some very subtle grey accents. I'm fine with that, as the focus is on performance and comfort.

Any extra aesthetic fancies are likely to add to the weight, which isn't worth the sacrifice for this kind of mouse. As with most ultralight mice, you know what you're getting aesthetically, and it's minimal.

This mouse uses the same software as the previous V2 Pro. What's noteworthy is the software is browser-based—there's no locally-installable app to use. That's mainly because you're expected to just set it and go, without returning to adjust things.

You can set up profiles to toggle between DPI using a mouse button combination, however. And the web software can be used offline if you install it as an app in your browser, so internet outages shouldn't cause any problems.

The web hub is basic but gets the job done. The battery indicator isn't very precise, only showing a tiny icon and no percentage numbers, but that's my only complaint.

The AimLabs integration is perfectly fine, too. Assuming you've got it installed on Steam, you can allow the web hub to boot it up for you from there, or boot it up yourself. Once in, you can navigate to PureVector and let it run you through the aim training to adjust your sensitivity in different sweep directions. It's intuitive, and the directional charts it shows are clear enough.

At $180/£160, the Sabre V3 Pro PureVector Ergo is an expensive mouse. It joins the likes of the G Pro X2/X3 Superstrike, Viper V4 Pro, DeathAdder V4 Pro, SteelSeries Rival Pro, and other high-end, competitive gaming mice.

Can it compete with these? In my opinion, not quite. These other gaming mice each have extra features and new technologies that go some way towards justifying the very high price tags. The Superstrikes have analogue clicks, the Viper V4 Pro has FrameSync, the Rival Pro has hot-swappable batteries and UWB connectivity.

The DeathAdder V4 Pro doesn't have anything too fancy like that, but is a very solid gaming mouse. I'd class the Sabre V3 Pro PureVector in this category, alongside the DeathAdder. That's because while the PureVector technology is indeed very new, I haven't found it to have much of an impact, and so I'm left considering its merits as a general competitive gaming mouse, setting aside this new aim assist tech.

There are merits to it that justify a price tag above $100: light weight, comfy ergonomic shape, optical clicks, responsive scroll wheel, great battery life. But not enough to justify $180—not without something extra, which PureVector promises but, in my case, fails to deliver. Unless, that is, you're set on getting a mouse as light as this one is that still has a sturdy shell.

You could instead, for instance, go for something like the Mchose K7 V2 Ultra+ for about $90. Or a Pulsar mouse like the Pulsar X2 CrazyLight for $130, which sometimes drops to about $100 on sale.

If you fancy spending the extra to try it out for yourself and see if you can get the kinds of benefits the pros that Corsair highlights espouse, go for it. But for my money, I'd be opting for a cheaper lightweight mouse, or one with better build quality like the Viper V4 Pro.

#3785. Firaxis reportedly cuts a third of its staff as studio head departs and new XCOM struggles

Civilization and XCOM developer Firaxis Games has laid off around 60 people.

The cuts, which took place today, account for about a third of the studio’s staff, Bloomberg reports, citing people familiar with the matter. Studio head Heather Hazen is also leaving.

Its sources say Firaxis' unannounced XCOM game has faced development struggles and missed "a significant milestone over the summer". The project will continue, but "may face a shakeup as a result of the cuts".

A spokesperson for 2K, the Take-Two label that runs Firaxis, confirmed Hazen's departure to Bloomberg, and said the studio is "restructuring and recentering around the studio's core strength - designing world class strategy games that have set the industry standard for the genre for the last 30 years".

"As part of these changes, the size of the studio is being reduced to focus on design, technology and the player experience, which means saying goodbye to talented colleagues who helped build Firaxis," the spokesperson continued. "These decisions are never easy, but they’re essential to build the next chapter of Firaxis."

The layoffs come two days before the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6, which is developed and published by Rockstar, a separate label at Take-Two.

In September, around 18 months after Civ 7's widely criticised launch - and as the legendary 4X series celebrates its 35th anniversary - Firaxis unveiled a host of new updates coming to the game as it continued to improve it. These included an atomic age update, dragging Civ 7 into the present and beyond, as well as its first paid expansion, Earthrise, both arriving next year.

Take-Two boss Strauss Zelnick admitted earlier this year that the studio "got it wrong with Civ 7".

"The game is a really good game. And it's certainly a profitable enterprise for us. But this is one where I think what we tried to do was a bridge too far, from the consumer's perspective," he told Game File in May.

It’s not the first round of cuts at the studio - 2K confirmed an unspecified number of layoffs at Firaxis in September 2025, and around 30 jobs went in 2023.

Nicolas Cage and Christian Bale may seem like two very different kinds of actors, but they do have something in common. They both truly commit to their roles no matter how bonkers or over-the-top they are. Bale and Cage have played characters who’ve gone bananas on screen, and that’s also the case with their latest movie, Madden. In the sports biopic, Cage and Bale play John Madden and Al Davis, respectively and wear a lot of prosthetics for the roles. And, as CinemaBlend learned, that’s surprisingly how their co-stars met them.

David O. Russell’s Madden – one of the buzzy titles on the 2026 movie schedule – chronicles the life and career of the titular football coach-turned-commentator. Cage really got into the role, and his physical transformation alone is proof of that. The same can be said for Bale, who’s known to transform by gaining or losing weight. So what’s it like to actually see the pair on set and in their element? Well, I recently spoke to co-stars Sienna Miller and Kathryn Hahn about that, and Miller shared a funny story about meeting Bale as Al:

I met Christian for the first time, decked out as Al. He came to say hi, which was very very exciting, and he was like, you know, [mimics Al Davis’ voice] ‘We're gonna have fun doing this,’ you know? And he's all in the voice, and I was beside myself, because I think he's really the GOAT, but then he's very funny on set and loves to play. And I'd imagined a real intensity, and there is once he's performing. But he loves to have a laugh off, you know, in between, and was not as you know — I think as actors, we're like a bunch of kids in a fancy dress cupboard, and that's what it felt like on this.

Miller plays the role of Carol Sagal Davis – the wife of late Oakland Raiders owner Al Davis – so she and Bale spent quite a bit of time together on set. For me, the mere thought of meeting Bale when he’s not in character seems intimidating, so I can’t even fathom the idea of being introduced to him while he’s decked out in prosthetics. What also has me chuckling is the thought of the Oscar winner keeping his character’s distinct accent while introducing himself to Miller. Nevertheless, it sounds like the two got along just fine.

During my recent interview, of course, I was also shocked to hear about Kathryn Hahn – who plays Virginia Fields Madden – meeting Nic Cage for the first time on set while he was under all of that heavy makeup. And, believe it or not, at the time we spoke, Hahn said she had never even been in Cage’s presence when he wasn’t in costume and prosthetics. She explained:

We were just saying that I've never seen Nic not as John Madden, so it's going to be so weird to finally be like, ‘Nice to meet you.’.... It's not like he was like a method actor, but there was a way of being that he instantly just filled out whenever he would put those prosthetics on. So yeah, that was the first time I met him was as John Madden, basically.

Something I can’t help but wonder is whether Cage’s Longlegs co-stars ever met him when he wasn’t dressed as the titular serial killer. I can’t imagine Cage sparking unease on set whenever he wasn’t giving that creepy and perfect performance. Yet I can definitely admit I’d still be genuinely creeped out just by being in his presence.

But, as for Madden, I can imagine those on-set interactions being memories that neither Hahn nor Miller will ever forget. Speaking of these two talented actresses, they also wear prosthetics at different points in the movie, though they arguably aren’t as extensive as those of their on-screen partners. Still, like Cage and Bale, Miller and Hahn fully commit to their roles as well, delivering some humorous performances in the process.

Now, if anything I just want to know what it was like when Kathryn Hahn and Nicolas Cage finally met at the Madden premiere. I’m tempted to assume that was a fun moment. But, that aside, check out the movie, which is playing in select theaters and streaming with a Prime Video subscription.

#3783. Chronicles: Medieval devs Raw Power are bankrupt, but their sandbox RPG lives on at a new studio co-founded by Satisfactory devs Coffee Stain

It "ticks many of the boxes", despite the funding problems

Goat Simulator and Satisfactory outfit Coffee Stain Group have bought the intellectual property rights and assets for Chronicles: Medieval, the Tom Hardy-garnished strategy RPG that was originally in development at now-bankrupt Raw Power Games. The game will now be made by a new developer, owned 25% by a few former Raw Power devs and 75% by Coffee Stain. Coffee Stain will fund the game's on-going development.

In development since 2022, and slated for Steam early access release in 2027, Chronicles: Medieval is a game about building vast armies of men in metal hats and horrifying doublets, then fighting alongside them in real time. It sees you positioning archers behind spears and finessing your cavalry flanking actions, all the while occupying a fleshy human body that can be hacked and stabbed. It's set during the Hundred Years' War between England and France over the 14th and 15th centuries, and gives you a volatile sandbox world of warring factions and patrols.

The original devs included people who worked on The Witcher 3, Total War, and Crusader Kings III, which may not surprise you from the foregoing descriptions. It's not entirely clear who has made the leap to Coffee Stain's newly founded studio.

Raw Power declared bankruptcy on 30th October, subsequently calling on players to help them find funding. During the bankruptcy proceedings, Coffee Stain successfully bid 36.75 million Danish Krone for Chronicles: Medieval, which comes to around four million pounds or 5.4 million dollars. According to CEO Anton Westbergh the project "ticks many of the boxes that we believe to be fundamental for a great game, and we think it has a good chance of becoming a strong long-term IP for the group." The game yet sits at 26th on SteamDB's most wishlisted, despite Raw Power's funding troubles.

Gaming doesn't want for simulations of shrieking feudal folk, but Medieval has a certain swagger, even when you remove Tom Hardy from the picture (and you should - he only ever voiced that one trailer). Here's hoping the new team can find their feet under Coffee Stain, and that whoever hasn't made the transition finds good work elsewhere.

I just found a curious artifact of the Old West in GTA 6, and the best part is I stumbled across it completely by accident.

That's right, partner: Arthur Morgan's cowboy hat is in Grand Theft Auto 6, and you won't find it in some trendy Western fashion shop or in a McMansion as part of a wealthy crypto bro's collection.

If you want to wear it yourself, I'll tell you below where you can find it.

I was out in Port Gellhorn looking for a particular kind of car for reasons completely unrelated to clothing accessories. While I was driving, I spotted a sign on the side of the road with a balloon tied to it, reading "Yard Sale" with an arrow pointing down the road.

I followed the sign which led to more yard sale signs and, yup, sure enough, the signs pointed me to an actual yard sale. And among the items for sale was a very familiar-looking hat.

It's called a "Genuine Cowboy Hat" and, this being a yard sale, it only cost $5. But I knew the second I saw it that this was no ordinary cowboy hat. Here, have a look at it from the back.

Yep. No mistaking that. I even got a little pang of sadness thinking about good ol' Arthur Morgan. I miss him. Maybe when I'm done with GTA 6, I'll strap on my spurs and take another ride through Red Dead Redemption 2.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Directions: Head to Port Gellhorn. It's in Kelly County on the western side of the state along the coast. In the southern tip of Port Gellhorn, there's a small neighborhood of about five houses just northwest of the Dirt Merchants mod shop.

Look for the driveway filled with yard sale clutter: furniture and electronics and such. There's a bunch of balloons, a cut-out of a nearly naked cowboy, and a big American flag flying. You'll find the hat toward the back sitting on top of a guitar case on a couch. There's also a shirt, a cap, and some shoes for sale that definitely didn't belong to Arthur.

#3781. The Game Awards 2026 nominees announced, and GTA 6 leads with eight nods before it's even out

The Game Awards 2026 nominees have been revealed, and Grand Theft Auto 6 leads the pack with eight nominations, two days before it even launches.

Rockstar's crime epic is up for Game of the Year, Best Game Direction, Best Narrative, Best Art Direction, Best Score and Music, Best Audio Design, and Best Action/Adventure Game. Its eighth nomination is Manni L. Perez's Best Performance nod for her role as Lucia, which is how we found out who plays her in the first place.

THE GAME AWARDS: 2026 Nominee Reveal! (Game of the Year) THE GAME AWARDS: 2026 Nominee Reveal!Watch on YouTube

For Game of the Year, GTA 6 is up against 007 First Light, Control Resonant, Phantom Blade Zero, Resident Evil Requiem, and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Nintendo is the most-nominated publisher, with 12 nominations across its games, followed by Capcom with 11, and Annapurna Interactive and PlayStation with nine each.

The nominees were picked by a jury of more than 160 media and creator outlets, who may get advance or pre-release access to games - which explains how GTA 6 made the cut before launch. The winners will be revealed on Thursday, 10th December, at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles. Fans can vote on The Game Awards' website until 6pm PT on 9th December.

This year's show will stream for free on more than 40 platforms, including YouTube, Twitch, Prime Video, and Steam. Last year's show drew an estimated 171 million livestreams, up 11 percent on 2024's 154 million.

#3780. SteamDB will add "affiliate links to authorised game retailers" and a new tab dedicated to mods, first update since Nexus Mods takeover confirms

"We're still in the early stages of what we want to achieve"

In a first substantial update since acquiring SteamDB from its founders back in September, the owners of Nexus Mods have outlined some new additions coming to , the two sides in the deal have announced some additions coming to the community-run backend database. Affiliate links aimed at providing options to help folks find the cheapest price for a game and a new tab dedicated to the mods Nexus host for a game are incoming, as work on behind-the-scenes improvements continues.

"We're now a couple of months in since [the takeover] announcement, so I thought it was about time we shared a quick update on what we've been working on behind the scenes, along with a few changes you'll start to see rolling out over the coming weeks," Victor Folmann, CEO of Nexus Mods owners Chosen wrote in a blog post on SteamDB.

There are two main new features he pointed to that you'll notice popping up on SteamDB soon. The first is one that anyone could have seen coming, a new tab on each moddable game's page that shows off some mods hosted for it on Nexus Mods and a host of modding-related data. "The new tab will help you discover mods for games you're browsing on SteamDB, making it easier to see whether a game has an active modding community and explore what it has to offer," Fomann wrote. "For now, we'll only be showing mods from Nexus Mods, as we already have access to that wealth of modding data, making it a straightforward starting point for this new feature.

"We appreciate that some of you might be wondering why we're not including Steam Workshop, too. It's certainly something we'd be open to exploring as we develop the feature further, along with other modding sources. With that in mind, if you run a modding website and would be interested in having your community's mods included, we'd love to hear from you."

That seems perfectly fine, but the other incoming feature's a bit more controversial given SteamDB's historically not been all about the money. "One thing we've seen people ask for is an easier way to find the cheapest place to buy a game, and we're now working on making that possible," Folmann wrote. "We'll be introducing affiliate links to authorised game retailers, giving you more options when looking for the best available price on a game.

"We recognise that introducing affiliate links may raise some concerns, so we want to be clear about how they'll work. First and foremost, as I mentioned, we'll only feature authorised retailers; we will not be including grey-market resellers. We've also made a deliberate decision about how prices are displayed: retailers will be ordered by the cheapest available price in your currency, not by whichever retailer offers us the highest affiliate commission. If a retailer doesn't offer pricing in your currency, we'll still show deals in other currencies provided they are available in your region."

Folmann was clear in the initial announcement of the takeover that Nexus Mods' bosses would be actively looking into ways SteamDB could make more money to sustain itself, so the addition of these links isn't out of the blue either. Whether SteamDB regulars agree that they're a "lighter-touch" way of earning the site some cash without detracting from the traditional experience of using it is another matter. I'll need to see how I feel once I've actually navigated a few pages with the links in as part of looking up stuff about games, but my first instinct is that as long as the pages don't end up revolving around the links and it's still easy to get to the info you want without interacting with them, I probably won't be too put out.

Beyond those tweaks, Folmann mentioned "improvements to how updates are tested before they go live" and how quickly the team can react to issues have been among the less obvious work going on behind the scenes. "We're still in the early stages of what we want to achieve, and there's plenty more work we need to do and would like to work on," he wrote in closing.

Folmann and co only took over Nexus Mods in June last year, making them still relatively new custodians of both it and SteamDB.

It’s a common practice for celebrity couples to keep their private lives, well private, and it’s no different for Zendaya and Tom Holland. While the two choose to keep things private, they understand the “parasocial investment” fans have in their relationship. However, even big-name directors can’t help sharing funny relationship stories about them, such as dishing about Holland’s funny reaction to seeing Zendaya in The Odyssey, and it’s just too perfect.

Director Christopher Nolan continued to praise Zendaya’s performance when he sat down with Stephen Spielberg during a special screening of The Odyssey. However, this time around he shared what her husband’s reaction was to seeing her play a goddess, and it’s probably not what you think. During the Q&A (via People) in West Hollywood, California, Nolan revealed there was a moment that got a little too real for Holland:

You have his vision of Athena made by Zendaya. I mean, she just gives him this look of disappointment. When Tom Holland saw the film, he’s like, ‘I know that look. I don’t like it.’ It’s an uncomfortable sensation. She’s incredible in the part. I mean, to have the two of them on that boat playing that moment together.

Now, Holland did have a front-row seat to watch her work her magic. The spouses may not have shared a scene in The Odyssey, but that doesn’t mean they weren’t together on set. Zendaya previously shared during a Los Angeles special screening Q&A that Holland helped calm her nerves on her first day. Her husband sat off to the side in a corner, reminding her, “You got this.”

Additionally, this isn’t the first time Nolan has praised Zendaya. Her co-star Matt Damon previously shared that after calling cut for one of their scenes, Nolan only had one word for her performance: “Perfect.” This led to a playful competition between Damon and Holland to see if they could match that Zendaya excellence. The scene that reveals Athena in a vision of Odysseus, where she appears as a guide, is so good that Spielberg also sang her praises:

It was wonderful, but she was also kind of a therapeutic companion. She just was there accompanying him. It was great accompaniment. And I thought she was wonderful. I think everybody was wonderful in the movie.

The high praise is valid, as there’s good reason why Nolan chose Zendaya to play the goddess of wisdom. You just have to look at this past year alone to see how versatile she is, and she’s not even done. She still has the upcoming Dune: Part Three hitting the 2026 schedule on December 18 and will also be heard in the upcoming fifth Shrek movie.

The actor previously shared her desire to take time off after a busy year. However, a recent announcement has her in the cast of a currently untitled Alex Garland sci-fi project from A24. The details for the movie are scarce, though I'm sure whenever filming begins, Holland will be in a corner on set cheering her on.

Let’s just hope he doesn’t have to see ‘that look’ again.

#3778. Former GTA 4 and Red Dead boss thinks "we are one Toy Story moment away" from people accepting gen-AI in game development in the West

"In the East, they've already accepted it."

Ben Feder, the former Take-Two CEO who oversaw the launch of massive hits like Grand Theft Auto 4, Red Dead Redemption, Borderlands, and BioShock during his tenure, believes the resistance against gen-AI in games will vanish once the games industry has its 'Toy Story moment'.

"When animation went from hand-drawn to computer animation, there was a massive wall of resistance," Feder told The Game Business. "People didn't think it looked good. Then Pixar launched Toy Story. They created a movie that not only was awesome, but used computer-generated animation and chose a subject matter that made the most of it, and did an amazing job with it."

Feder argued that the success of Toy Story ended the resistance against computer-generated animation, and the same could happen to games. Feder added, "My own view is that we are one Toy Story moment away from consumer acceptance of AI in video games in the West. In the East, they've already accepted it."

Feder, who currently heads up venture capital fund Tirta Ventures, is investing in AI-first games. He, however, doesn't necessarily believe AI will reduce development costs, but that it also offers other advantages that could help game makers keep up with shifting consumer tastes.

"A lot of incumbents think about AI as a way of reducing costs, which it is," Feder said. "I query whether it will actually reduce costs, or will it just make games bigger for the same cost? But we're more interested in what AI can do to radically change gameplay."

Feder views gen-AI simply as new technology that allows developers to do things they couldn't before. He likened it to Unreal Engine's instancing technology, which allowed Fortnite and other battle royale games to support 100+ players in a single server.

"That's question number one as we think about what we invest in: Was this possible before AI?" Feder said of his VC firm's strategy. "And when AI gets better, does the game get better? That's harder for an incumbent to focus on, because they deploy a lot of capital, have enormous advantages in terms of distribution, capital, and IP, and all of that needs to be protected."

There's been enormous pushback from players, developers and pundits against the use of gen-AI in games. Even so, more and more studios have revealed using some gen-AI during development, such as to assist with coding. More broadly, gen-AI adoption is on the rise across the industry, with a recent report estimating 40 percent of developers are using it.

Some development studios, such as Fortnite maker Epic Games, have doubled down on the use of gen-AI in game development. Epic is even more bullish on gen-AI in its Unreal Engine, which the company is currently transforming into an engine that's almost entirely driven by gen-AI and LLMs. Consumer sentiment remains sour, however, and the perception of the tool is not helped by the number of 'AI slop' games taking over Steam's storefront, the 'enshittification' of fan wikis, or the link AI seems to have to the unprecedented wave of layoffs that has shaken the industry over the past two years.

David Fincher and Quentin Tarantino prove a perfect match in this Once Upon A Time in… Hollywood spin-off that centers Brad Pitt's Oscar-winning stuntman. Does it need to exist? Not really. But we're glad it does.

Fincher knows how to direct Tarantino's peerless dialogue

Pitt's as good here as he was in …Hollywood.

Rick Dalton's absence is awkwardly handled

Why you can trust GamesRadar+ Our experts review games, movies and tech over countless hours, so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about our reviews policy.

A Netflix sequel to 2019's Once Upon A Time in… Hollywood that drops Rick Dalton and Sharon Tate for further Cliff Booth misadventures is an undeniably odd proposition. But this David Fincher-directed, Quentin Tarantino-written follow-up plays to both their strengths, and proves that Brad Pitt is never better than when working with his movie-making soulmates.

Unburdened from the self-inflicted pressure to make his tenth and final movie a career-capping magnum opus, this is Tarantino’s most playful and straightforwardly enjoyable script since Jackie Brown. In fact, there's a lot of Elmore Leonard in this late-70s Hollywood hangout movie that only occasionally detours into criminal activity; little surprise that Tarantino has also penned the novelization releasing next month.

Plot-light but chock-full of memorable scenes, exchanges and characters, it might not have the thematic depth of its predecessor, which explored the difficult transition to the Hollywood New Wave for outdated stars like Rick Dalton (and their stuntmen). Neither does it really reckon with OUATIH's revisionist fairytale ending by focusing so squarely on Cliff. But Pitt's ceaselessly cool, sociopathic alpha dude is a blast to be reacquainted with.

Set over a matter of days, some 8 years after averting a Manson Family massacre, Cliff is now back working odd jobs around L.A. after Rick upped sticks to Sydney for a starring role in the successful Aussie series Dingo Dan. Still something of a fixer for his friends, resourceful war hero Cliff is approached by A-list movie star Charlie Peters (Scott Caan, looking more like his dad by the day) not to double for him, but to solve a problem involving a pair of Filipino brothers whom Charlie has accidentally hired to murder his wife, Tony (Carla Gugino).

Release date: November 25 (IMAX), December 23 (Netflix)Available: In theaters and NetflixDirector: David FincherWriter: Quentin TarantinoRuntime: 2h 20m

Also central is Peters' agent, Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki) – an Aussie immigrant and former film critic who Cliff, of course, has the hots for. It's been a minute since a proper Tarantino romance (if you don't count Cliff and Rick's bromance in OUATIH), and Cliff's playful pursuit of kinky Karen fizzes like a classic Bogart and Bacall pairing. Former RoboCop Peter Weller is also something of a scene-stealer as Cliff's grumpy but loving dad.

What you might be wondering is what Fight Club director David Fincher brings to the table, and the answer is a lot. Like the peanut butter and chocolate pairing of Fincher and Sorkin on The Social Network, the two filmmaking titans operate surprisingly harmoniously here. Fincher's ice-cold technical precision is best exemplified in the depiction of the killer Verdusco brothers. One early home invasion sequence is shockingly brutal and recalls the matter-of-fact violence of Zodiac. While, like OUATIH, the movie builds to an explosive action set-piece that is ferocious, unforgettable and sends you out on a gleeful high.

Despite everything The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth has going for it, there is still a niggling sense that it's somewhat superfluous as an exercise. Would all this time, money and effort not be better spent on anything other than a side-story involving a Tarantino supporting character? As if to head off the accusation, Cliff at one point asks Karen, "You might be wondering, why all of it?" The answer: "I'm not that deep." And neither is the film. It's a romp, a caper, a good time that luxuriates in the texture of late 70s Hollywood but doesn't have an awful lot to say beyond 'Isn't this a great place to spend 140 minutes?'

Pitt's ceaselessly cool, sociopathic alpha dude is a blast to be reacquainted with.

There are some fun cameos to watch out for: Timothy Olyphant returns as Rick Dalton's old Bounty Law co-star, James Stacy, for a terrific scene that takes Tarantino back into Inglourious Basterds territory. And Caan makes an electric return to movies as A-lister Peters, whose voluminous ego overcompensates for his diminutive stature – a tragedy Caan was stuck on the Hawaii Five-0 reboot for a decade. But Yahya Abdul-Mateen II is underutilized as blacksploitation star Rodrick 'Hot Rod' Harrison, and Leonardo DiCaprio's Dalton is conspicuous by his absence; Tarantino's script is on shakiest ground when repeatedly trying to justify his nonappearance.

The beneficiary of Narnia's 3-month delay, The Further Mis-Adventures… is getting a two-week release on IMAX screens before it heads to Netflix. Despite my (limited) misgivings, the big(gest) screen is the format to seek out, as it's the type of film where full immersion relies on undivided attention. Plus, you'd be mad to pass up the opportunity to see a Fincher-directed, Erik Messerschmidt-shot movie on the best screen possible. Whether or not we'll get Tarantino's tenth and final movie anytime soon is unclear as the search continues for the perfect swan song. But, in the meantime, more Tarantino scripts making their way into the hands of filmmakers like David Fincher can only be a good thing.

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth plays on IMAX screens for two weeks from November 25, and releases on Netflix from December 23. For more, here are the most exciting upcoming movies heading our way across the rest of the year, and beyond.

#3776. "It’s hard not to worry": Even as GTA 6 launches on console amid glowing reviews, Rockstar devs are already concerned about getting laid off

Even though they've "had no indication that layoffs are coming" from bosses

GTA 6 launches on console today. It's widely expected to sell more copies than main character Lucia Caminos has skin pores, more copies than there are words even in Eurogamer's five-star review, which I believe Chris Tapsell has written specifically to exhaust and destroy such neurones as I have remaining. And yet, staff at Rockstar Games are apparently worrying about being laid off, as development winds down and investors start to bicker about Line Going Up Even More.

In an article supporting this month's union vote at Rockstar North, one of the game's animation programmers argues that "workers across the sector are helpless to resist the waves of redundancies crashing around us, until we get organised."

The animation programmer in question is Nestor Uriarte, writing in The Guardian's Comment Is Free section. Following some personal reflections on his time at the studio, he calls on other Rockstar devs to get behind the union, describing it as both "a huge step forward" for a company that has previously faced allegations of "crunch culture", and a win for UK game developers at large. "What happens here could open the door for other workers across the UK to imagine an alternative future for the industry – one in which workers’ voices are taken into account more," Uriarte writes.

The vote at Rockstar North will run till 26th November, and could give rise to a union spanning over 1600 developers, according to umbrella organisation the Independent Workers of Great Britain. If that comes to pass, it would make the Rockstar union the largest recognised videogame developer union in the UK.

It comes as the company and a group of fired workers await the result of an employment tribunal battle over alleged "union-busting". Rockstar has accused the workers in question of "gross misconduct" and a breach of confidentiality by means of a union Discord server. Amongst other things, the legal brawl has revealed that Rockstar had a mole on that server for two and a half years, prior to the firings.

As for the prospect of further job losses, after GTA 6 goes on sale, Uriarte cites a wave of mass layoffs across the industry that has affected the creators of even commercially successful games like Battlefield 6 and Netflix's FIFA World Cup.

"After the big day, we have had no indication that layoffs are coming, but it’s hard not to worry about what the future holds," he writes. "Studios across the industry have been slashing huge portions of their workforces, with an estimated 24,000 roles axed globally over the last two years. It says a lot about the industry that even my colleagues and I, working on the biggest game of all time, are worried about getting laid off. But the truth is that workers across the sector are helpless to resist the waves of redundancies crashing around us, until we get organised."

The obvious context here is that GTA 6 has been a massively expensive production, with a development team headcount in the thousands. While one could accuse Uriarte of fear-mongering, I do find it hard to believe that executives at parent company Take-Two aren't weighing up some timely "down-sizing" right now. In general, videogame companies have a long tradition of axing the books once a game has been shipped, despite arguments that keeping experienced teams intact often pays off. In Rockstar's case, however, it's also worth bearing in mind that the GTA 6 rolling out this week is only part of the package. There's also the hazy prospect of the next incarnation of GTA Online, which – going by GTA 5 sales – will be a money spinner for many years, and will require a sizeable staff to maintain. Oh, and of course there's the PC version.

Echoing many peers, Uriarte also argues in his piece that it's important to unionise now in order to negotiate proper protection against generative AI cost-cutting initiatives. "The rapid emergence of AI is transforming how studios work and raising fundamental questions about the future of our industry," he continues. "Across the sector, the skills that workers spend years developing risk being devalued as their creative work is replaced by AI.

"Rockstar has said it is committed to preserving jobs and it has been clear that our games will continue to be made by people," Urirarte concedes. "But with recognition we’d have a seat at the table to manage this industry-wide transition together."

#3775. I have double-checked and yes, original 'GTA killer' Driv3r really was that rubbish

At this point the tragedy of Driv3r, or Driver 3, or my personal favourite Drive-thrur, is well thumbed. A familiar litany of unrealised ambition, heinous bugs, dull open-world design, and an expensive yet audibly bored voice cast, the accidental comedic highlight of which is Michelle Rodriguez flatly reeling off car theft orders from what sounds like the inside of a Michelle Rodriguez-sized tupperware container.

A more widely forgotten detail is that, for a while, there was a non-zero chance - a belief, even - that Drive Three Er was going to be the opposite. The 2003-2004 hype cycle had sowed the notion that this would in fact be the open-world crime thriller to knock Grand Theft Auto off its perch, and even 22 years before GTA 6's idolising reviews, that was no small promise; Rockstar were still enjoying the balmy success of Vice City, and we could see San Andreas cresting the hill on a stolen, shining BMX. "Ah, but did they have Michael Madsen doing doughnuts in car parks?," publishers Atari asked the world, either unaware or in denial of the spluttering, clapped-out rattletrap they were about to wheel into the showroom.

You likely know the rest, though one of the dangers of familiarity is the subsequent breeding of complacency, which in this case can manifest as a thawing acceptance. I succumbed to this myself, having recently installed a legally unlinkable copy of Drivethreeuh, mind opened to the possibility that maybe it wasn't that bad. Six hours later, I am here to tell you: it was.

Almost nothing here works, figuratively and literally. Within three minutes of the opening mission, before Madsen's undercover cop Tanner goes undercover, you're ordered to join some marked police cars to head for a bust – but because the rozzers' primary function is to give chase to you, later on, driving too close crosses their wires, provoking them into blue-on-blue ramming maneuvres. Later, in a motorbike sprint down an inexplicably exploding beach, cartel goons are positioned across the sand, presumably to take drama-enhancing pot shots. They're so slow, however, both to notice your presence and to physically raise their guns, that they're barely out of their idle animations by the time you whizz past. And your own guy isn't much better: an assassination mission, which ends with your target cornered from an elevated position, requires that you take a few steps backwards first, as Tanner can't drop his shootin' arms low enough to land a hit from the balcony he's on.

Unlike Vice City's Tommy Vercetti, he can at least swim, which by 2004 standards gives the seaside Miami and Nice maps a fair verisimilitude, particularly when a shot-up boat engine forces the abandoning of ship. No amount of product-of-its-time concessions, though, can account for how woodenly unpalatable the on-foot action is. Controls are stiff and shooting feels meaningless, with zero tangible sense of bullets being sent nor received; killing a man carries all the weight of just shouting at him to lie down, and if it weren't for sound effects and the dwindling health bar, I could park Tanner in front of a firing squad of identically-modelled thugs with almost zero impression that his lungs were filling with Uzi rounds.

Driver, of course, began as a pure wheelman sim, later installments only letting you hoof it after someone at developers Reflections began smelling that Rockstar money. It was therefore always unlikely, even for the purported GTA killer, that this would achieve action-adventure sophistication in its bipedal bits. Even so, god, it's woeful. Stingy checkpointing also means that failure is often punished by having to replay those tedious, flavourless shootouts in full.

The driving is better, which is a bit like saying there's decent cheese in this cheese and smallpox toastie. It's reasonably slidey, when throwing the back end through a curving French alleyway, and in contrast to the gunplay, there is a somewhat realised tactility to ploughing around in two tonnes of rolling metal. It has problems of its own, mind. Cars feel okay when they're moving, but contact and crashes are leaden, sluggish, visually underwhelming occasions that I would call non-events, were they not so slow to recover from that a single nasty impact can scupper a timed mission. Granted, I quickly re-learned how vital it is to keep both eyes on the road, as other vehicles, pedestrians, lamposts, and other detritus tend to pop into existence some mere fifty feet in front of my speeding bumper.

The result, of both this graphical shortcoming and the overly punishing crashes, is a getaway car sim that too often encourages you to drive like cataract-ridden grandparent. Worse, whoever put Letty Ortiz in a lunchbox must have also been in charge of the engine noises, producing an array of miserable high-rev dins – especially for the motorbikes, which screech like amateurishly autotuned vacuum cleaners. There are also shades of that deranged cop AI in ordinary commuters, who I've repeatedly seen swerving and slaloming around empty lanes, seemingly for no reason beyond violent confusion.

Strangely enough, my 2026 return has largely dodged the game's infamous glitchiness, the worst instance of physics defiance being a garage door that appeared to lift Tanner into the air before propelling him, incorporeally, through the car shed's roof. I recall much worse, from the days when I'd have my dad rent it for me from Blockbuster. Mission-critical NPCs getting stuck on walls; flipped pursuit cars spinning endlessly; getting flung into space when walking on an overturned vehicle (a common occurrence, given the actual 'crawling out' animation sometimes failed to play, the game instead teleporting you onto the spring-loaded underside instead).

I've thus far escaped these, but as far as I know, they're still lurking dormant, and none of what I've witnessed with adult eyes has been funny or stupid enough to imbue Driv3r 3 The Third with a Wiseauean so-bad-it's-good quality. It's just bad. It was always bad. Why did I even entertain the possibility that it wasn't bad?

Reflections, to their credit, accepted their folly. Narratively unrelated sequel Driver: Parallel Lines tucked away a bin full of discarded copies, at least until Ubisoft bought up the series and patched it out, and for all the fantastical coma silliness of direct followup Driver: San Francisco, that was sensible enough to keep Tanner where he best belongs: hands on the wheel, foot on the gas, gun holstered. And was a far, far better game for it, too.

As 2011's San Francisco launch also remains the most recent Driver release, I regretfully can't end with the assurance that DrIIIver's legacy is a mere blip on a redeemed franchise. That stain stank, and did for ages, very possibly to the extent that GTA's one-time biggest rival never recovered.

Still, even if Reflections couldn't fully turn around their fortunes, the consistent improvement from this to Parallel Lines to San Francisco showed that they did learn something. Maybe so too did anyone else who went on to make an open-world action game. Which wouldn't be the worst outcome; after all, those who do not learn from gnarled, stinking wrecks like this are doomed to repeat them.

#3774. "Abducting your own lover no longer gives you opinion of yourself" declare the notes for Crusader Kings 3's free Florin update, released alongside Silk and Silver

Funky feudal family frolic Crusader Kings 3 got its second major expansion of the year this week. It's called Silk and Silver (read my impressions), is all about merchant republics, and shipped alongside a beefy free update to the base game which - while largely focused on overhauling economics - also has some funny patch notes and features worth being aware of.

The main features of the free 'Florin' update are outlined by Paradox in the video above, and unless you're really into the nitty gritty details of realm and wealth management, there's one bit of it which stands out. The option to play as a landless adventurer has finally made its way into the base game, as Paradox promised earlier this year.

This means you can kick off a playthrough as a lowborn leader of a travelling band or a wandering noble with claims on realms ruled by others. Originally locked behind the Roads to Power DLC, the option to start off this way or end up living if you end up deposed from your throne of choice is a great addition to the story arc of any CK3 run. No longer are you glued to the throne from day one to the day you quit for good - power's a privilege which can be earned and revoked depending on what you get up to. Though, it's worth noting that only three ways of operating as a landless adventurer are being made free to access with this update. You can be an aimless wanderers, sword-toting mercenaries, or scholars. If you want your band to earn their living as explorers, free booters, or legitimists, you'll still need Roads to Power.

As for the rest of the free additions, community manager Jacob Blakey summed them up thusly:

As ever, I'm a bit sad that those are gone, even if they had to go.

If you're one of the countless millions contributing to the collective endangering of global productivity by enjoying Grand Theft Auto 6 at launch, you might have paused in the middle of blatantly disregarding traffic laws to wonder: Wait a second, am I hearing "Weird Al" Yankovic hosting this pretend radio station?

And yes, you are: In a Bluesky post earlier today, the beloved comedic musician and polka maestro confirmed that he offered his voice for DJ Al, who hosts '80s music station Vice City FM alongside Swedish actress, model, and singer Brigitte Nielsen. Their contributions were then double-confirmed by the full GTA 6 credits, which Rockstar published once launch time hit.

I’m the host of GTA 6’s “non-stop ‘80s” radio channel Vice City FM. I also wrote some in-game commercials, and I’m the voice of the Burger Shot ads as well! As a long-time fan of the Grand Theft Auto franchise, I couldn’t be more excited about this. Okay, gotta get back to playing the game!

"I’m the host of GTA 6’s 'non-stop ‘80s' radio channel Vice City FM. I also wrote some in-game commercials, and I’m the voice of the Burger Shot ads as well!" Yankovic said. "As a long-time fan of the Grand Theft Auto franchise, I couldn’t be more excited about this. Okay, gotta get back to playing the game!"

Somewhere out there, Weird Al is securing the love of his virtual latina wife, and I think that's beautiful.

Yankovic is just one of countless recognizable names you'll find if you scroll down the GTA 6 credits. Among the core cast, SNL alumnus Bobby Moynihan voices Cal, Jason's bumbling, conspiracy-brained buddy. The pair's criminal boss man, Brian Heder, is performed by legendary Stephen Root—who you'll likely recognize as Bill Dauterive on King of the Hill, Milton in Office Space, and all kinds of magnificent weirdos across the Coen brothers filmography.

But it's the radio talent where GTA 6's credits get particularly wild. It's a cavalcade of international music icons, comedians, and film figures. While driving around GTA 6, you might hear Lana Del Rey hosting Back Country Radio, or Latin music phenom Bad Bunny on Cocoteo FM. On Dirty South Classics, there's Trina, Trick Daddy, and Gucci Mane. Pop station Flash FM is helmed by Robyn and Alex Consani—the first transgender model to win Model of the Year at the British Fashion Awards and celebrated TikTok goofball. Keith Richards is in there. I didn't even know he was still capable of speech.

On talk radio, you can hear Ted Lasso's Jason Sudeikis, Abbot Elementary's Janelle James, and John Leguizamo of being John Leguizamo fame. Stavros Halkias is on there doing a Conservative talk radio bit. But maybe the most compelling inclusion, for me, is that Kaleidoscope FM is hosted by Jeremy Irons. The Academy Award-winning actor. You were in Kafka, Jeremy. How'd you end up in cyber-Florida?

If I wanted to include all the recognizable names on the list, I'd need a dozen more paragraphs, so I recommend you browse the credits yourself. Or just be content in knowing that Weird Al is waiting for you. That works for me, too.

#3772. Korridor turns those Youtube ads for vertical mobile shooters into a new, "deeply strategic" genre, and I can't decide if it's lying

The electro-metal OST seems legit, at least

I like to think I'm difficult to hypnotise, but I confess, I'm a sucker for those Youtube adverts for the mobile vertical shooters. You know the ones: boglins pour towards an auto-firing player, who must dodge about to grab upgrades while whittling down the horde. The player in the advert always does pretty well for 20 seconds, but ahhhh, then they get just a tiny bit overconfident, mistime how long it'll take them to erode the health of an ogre midboss, and: bam!

Show me one of those ads, and I'll always watch to the end in the hope that this time, the protagonist will Study The Blade, conquer their harmatia, and slay the damn ogre. I've never actually played any of the mobile shooters in question, mind you. I'm far too cultured for that, you dope! Except that I've just been playing the demo for Korridor, which is supposedly "based off" of the ads, but might as well be one of the games they're promoting, for all I know.

Per the Steam page, it claims to have turned the above advert format into a whole new "deeply strategic genre", the "gates shooter", by stirring in "elements of roguelikes and bullet heavens". I need somebody to authenticate whether this is a truthful statement, or developer TinyToad pulling a fast one. In the meantime, I'll say that 1) I have now managed to kill several ogres, 2) I like Korridor's electro-metal soundtrack.

In Korridor, you're a bald medieval monk garbed in Poundshop Adeptus Astartes platemail. You've woken up in a dungeon of mysterious provenance, and must walk very slowly down its corridors korridors while shooting and punching goblins, wraiths and demons hurrying the other way. Each enemy has a numerical health indicator, and the basic challenge is working out whether you can empty it before they walk into you – which costs you a proportionate amount of health, mitigated by armour. As you go, you'll walk through a choice of gates that grant buffs such as faster health regen, bullet penetration, or nippier horizontal motion.

The fact that you don't control how fast the monk trudges vertically allows the game to synch the onslaught pretty tightly to the thudding, growling score. It reminds me a little of Thumper, though it isn't nearly so invigoratingly malevolent. So far. At intervals, the beat thickens and all the enemies burst into a sprint, throwing their arms up and conveying the strong impression that they are more running away from something than running at you. There's clearly a dreadful entity at the far end of the dungeon. Perhaps it is another overdressed monk with an even bigger gun.

Is this how those mobile games actually work? If it is, then alas and alack, all is lost. I've finally succumbed to those adverts, and all it took was some disingenuous Steam copy promising to place them at a critical remove. Curse you, TinyToad. Curse you and your gates. If you were actually a toad, I'd step on you. Still, now that we've broken the ice, can you please make another game in which I get to play one of those gloating giantesses in Hero Wars? Because I know some people who dig that kind of thing.
